items.title: [bbc.com] Brazil activates protective measures after about 20 isolated Awá approach
items.content_html:
🪶 ✏️

About 20 Indigenous Awá living in isolation approached the Guajajara village of Tawari on Monday, November 16, in Arariboia Indigenous Territory, in the Brazilian state of Maranhão; they received yams and returned to the forest. Members of the Guajajara community recorded the encounter, and the organization Survival International shared the footage. The National Foundation for Indigenous Peoples (Funai) and Indigenous health personnel are in the area. The government activated an emergency coordination mechanism to assess the situation and health risks. Authorities said they are still assessing the initial information and that this isolated approach does not mean the Awá have abandoned their isolation. The reason for the visit has not been confirmed; Survival International linked it to pressure from illegal loggers, hunters, and ranchers on the territory. Local residents voiced concern about the thinness of some children and older people. There is also concern about the risk of infections, given the group’s limited exposure to common pathogens.

items.content_html:
🪶 ✏️

Ontario Power Generation (OPG), the province-owned utility, says the first of four small modular reactors planned for the Darlington site east of Toronto will miss its October 2030 operating target and exceed its previously disclosed C$7.7 billion cost estimate. OPG has not yet provided a revised schedule or estimated the size of the overrun. It expects to substantially complete a cost-and-schedule assessment by mid-2027. The utility attributed the risks in part to unfinished engineering work on the first-of-its-kind BWRX-300 design, which it said is affecting construction and supply-chain performance. The four-reactor project has a C$20.9 billion budget. The first unit is the first small modular reactor to begin construction in a G7 country. OPG says construction continues while it works with reactor designer GE Vernova Hitachi Nuclear Energy to complete the outstanding engineering work.

items.title: [winnipegfreepress.com] Federal memo warns freshwater pressures threaten Canada’s long-term security
items.content_html:
🪶 ✏️

An internal federal memo warns that growing pressure on freshwater supplies could harm Canada’s long-term security and prosperity. It says it is unclear whether the country can meet future needs as its cities and economy grow. The Canada Water Agency prepared the document for Environment Minister Julie Dabrusin as work proceeds on a national water security strategy. Dabrusin called the strategy a “mission critical priority” in response to Prime Minister Mark Carney’s request for cabinet priorities. The memo links water risks to climate change, pollution, population growth, overuse and aging infrastructure. Public consultation ran from Sept. 9 to Oct. 25, and the agency also consulted provincial, territorial and Indigenous partners. The memo calls for an assessment of water protection and sustainable management, including shared waters with the United States and global water risks. The 12-page memo was obtained through an access-to-information request, with some material withheld.

items.title: [euronews.com] Denmark ratifies Greenland pact, clearing way for expanded U.S. military presence
items.content_html:
🪶 ✏️

Denmark’s parliament on Nov. 19 ratified a security agreement with Greenland and the United States, clearing the final parliamentary hurdle for expanded U.S. military activity on the Arctic island. All 109 lawmakers present voted in favor after Greenland’s parliament approved the pact earlier in November. The Danish foreign ministry must now notify Washington by diplomatic note before the agreement takes effect; it does not require a U.S. Senate vote. The agreement, signed in New York on Sept. 22 by President Donald Trump, Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen and Greenlandic Prime Minister Jens-Frederik Nielsen, supplements a 1951 defense accord. It allows the United States to expand operations at Pituffik Space Base and establish defense areas at Narsarsuaq and Mestersvig, including for the proposed Golden Dome missile-defense system. The pact is to remain in force if Greenland becomes independent and reaffirms Danish sovereignty and Greenlanders’ right to self-determination. The deal followed months of tension after Trump repeatedly said the United States should control Greenland, at times refusing to rule out force. The agreement also restricts military installations to NATO members and aims to prevent China or Russia from gaining influence in strategic sectors. Danish Defense Minister Jeppe Bruus said work would begin on legislation to screen outside investment on security grounds and on plans for the new U.S. facilities.

items.title: [japantimes.co.jp] Climate change intensified Indonesia’s worst wildfires in a decade, study finds

A World Weather Attribution study published Friday found that a strong El Niño drove Indonesia’s severe rainfall shortfall this year, while human-caused climate change made temperatures during the August-to-October fire season about 1.6 degrees Celsius higher. Researchers said warming made hot, dry fire conditions about three times more likely, while El Niño cut seasonal rainfall by roughly half. Decades of deforestation and peatland drainage also left the landscape more vulnerable to ignition. The fires have spread hazardous haze across Indonesia and neighboring Southeast Asian countries. Nusantara Atlas, an independent monitoring platform, estimated that fires affected 2.88 million hectares from January through October. The Indonesian government had not confirmed that total or issued its own estimate. Researchers called for peatland restoration, stronger land protections and reduced fossil-fuel emissions. Fires were still burning, with smoke detected in eastern Kalimantan on Nov. 12.

items.title: [theguardian.com] EU proposes extra €45 billion Ukraine loan, faces fight over guarantees
items.content_html:
🪶 ✏️

The European Commission proposed on Nov. 18 an additional €45 billion loan for Ukraine in 2027, covering about two-thirds of a projected €70 billion funding gap. It would supplement the €90 billion EU loan already approved for 2026 and 2027; the new package allocates up to €25 billion for military needs and €20 billion for Ukraine’s state budget. Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said the funding was intended to strengthen Kyiv’s position in negotiations with Russia. Ukraine would repay the principal only after receiving Russian reparations. The EU would raise the money on capital markets, with its common budget guaranteeing the borrowing. Budget support would be conditional on Ukrainian reforms, including on the rule of law and corruption. The Commission also wants other international partners to cover the remaining €25 billion of Ukraine’s estimated needs. Approval faces resistance from Bulgaria, the Czech Republic, Hungary and Slovakia, which have signalled they do not want to join the financing. German Chancellor Friedrich Merz has pressed for all 27 EU members to share responsibility and linked the Ukraine financing to talks on the bloc’s next long-term budget; Slovakia’s Prime Minister Robert Fico called that approach “blackmail”. EU leaders are due to discuss the proposal at a Brussels summit on Nov. 26-27, and the budget guarantee requires unanimous member-state backing.

items.title: [cbc.ca] Alberta bill sets data-centre limits and well cleanup funds
items.content_html:
🪶 ✏️

Alberta introduced Bill 42 on Nov. 18, proposing new siting and water rules for large data centres and mandatory cleanup funding for every new oil and gas well. Centres using at least 10 megawatts would generally have to be at least 600 metres from homes and avoid top-quality or irrigated farmland; they would also face a near-zero cooling-water standard. The Alberta Utilities Commission would regulate the larger facilities. The province says about 30% of current proposals could be affected, while projects already far along in approvals or construction would be exempt. For new wells, companies would pay up to $50,000 initially and make equal annual payments for up to 10 years. The money would remain attached to the well if ownership changes. If a well becomes orphaned, its funding would go to the Orphan Well Association. The requirements are expected to cover wells drilled after April 1, 2027. The bill would also eliminate Alberta’s oil-sands emissions cap, which the province says is redundant with industrial carbon pricing.

items.title: [Macworld] Update: Microsoft offers explanation for day-long Internet outage
items.content_html:
🪶 ✏️

Macworld

Whether you’re using a Mac, iPhone, or – shudder – a PC, a major Microsoft outage has disrupted Outlook email and other Microsoft 365 services worldwide. The problems began on Thursday, November 12, and continued overnight into Friday, affecting businesses, schools and public services.

Microsoft said a server process had become overwhelmed, reducing capacity. Recovery proved difficult because some servers became unresponsive again as traffic returned. Features that depend on Exchange Online were particularly affected, although not every function within each Microsoft service stopped working.

A look at Downdetector and ThousandEyes Outages also showed complaints involving unrelated platforms. However, those reports don’t establish that every service was down or that they shared Microsoft’s underlying problem. Amazon told Macworld that AWS was operating normally. Some users also reported problems with iMessage, although Apple’s System Status page showed no corresponding outage at the time.

Microsoft reported signs of recovery as it restarted affected infrastructure and managed traffic, but had not provided a confirmed time for full restoration. The company had not established a final root cause and said there was no indication that malicious activity was responsible.

Settle in, and here’s hoping it’s fixed soon. You can track the Microsoft service health here, and we’ll keep this article updated as we learn more.

Update 4:17 am GMT / 11:17 pm ET: Final restoration confirmed

Microsoft confirmed that the Microsoft 365 outage had been resolved. The company claims the outage was caused by a technical problem associated with a network-capacity upgrade.

Recovery continues to be monitored.

Update 8:55 pm GMT / 3:55 pm ET: Network change blamed

Microsoft has apologized for the outage as it works to restore all systems to normal: “This was a technical issue not related to cyber or AI / agents. The incident was introduced by an issue during an earlier network capacity upgrade that surfaced following a recent network change. We have addressed the underlying issue and continue to restore service to remaining customers and regions.”

Update 11:45 am GMT / 6.45 am ET: Recovery underway

Microsoft says it has completed recovery actions in Asia-Pacific and this recovery work is being extended to other regions, as per the Guardian’s live blog.

Update 10:15 am GMT / 5.15 am ET: The U.K. has woken up to the Microsoft outage

Microsoft’s service disruption continued into Friday, November 13, affecting Outlook email and Microsoft 365 features that depend on Exchange Online.

The disruption has affected NHS communications, with reports of NHS trusts, including Evelina London, a children’s healthcare provider, unable to send or receive emails.

Elsewhere, police forces have confirmed that some online reporting forms could be affected, but their ability to answer and respond to 999 and 101 calls had not been compromised.

Schools have also reported communication problems and asked parents to telephone rather than email their child’s school.

Microsoft’s Friday morning advisory, via the University of Pennsylvania’s Microsoft incident-report feed, says most core Teams calling, meetings and messaging functionality is unaffected, although calendar and other email-dependent features can fail.

Microsoft reported early signs of stabilization on Friday morning, but said capacity had not returned to normal and recovery remained uneven.

Update 9:45 pm ET: “Positive results”

Microsoft reported “seeing positive results” with its efforts to correct the outage as it restarted affected infrastructure and brought servers back into service in isolation.

Update 4:39 pm ET: AWS is normal

An Amazon spokesperson reached out to Macworld to let us know that AWS is functioning normally and has been all day.

Any disruptions today would have to be caused by something else.

Update 2:00 pm ET: The whole Internet is having major issues right now

Whether you’re using a Mac, iPhone, or – shudder – a PC, you may be having trouble accessing Outlook email and other Microsoft 365 services.

Downdetector and ThousandEyes Outages are recording widespread reports of connectivity problems. Users have also reported issues with unrelated platforms, although those reports do not establish that every service is down or that they share the same underlying cause.

Some users are reporting problems with Apple services, including iMessage, but Apple’s System Status page shows no corresponding outage at the time of writing.

OpenAI and Anthropic have also reported disruption to the tools that connect their AI assistants to Microsoft 365. For ChatGPT users who connect Microsoft services, this could interrupt tasks that depend on retrieving information from those services.

The cause and expected restoration time remain unclear. We’ll update this live blog as providers confirm more information.

items.title: [Fast Company] DOJ sues Lyft for allegedly denying rides to people with disabilities
items.content_html:
🪶 ✏️

The Justice Department has filed a lawsuit against Lyft, accusing the company of discriminating against passengers with disabilities who seek rides on its platform.

The federal lawsuit, filed Monday, says Lyft “is aware of, but fails to prevent and remedy” several discriminatory practices against riders who need accommodations under the Americans With Disabilities Act. That includes denying rides to people who have service animals or use stowable wheelchairs and refusing to let passengers with mobility issues sit in the front seat, the suit alleges.

“Individuals with disabilities should be able to rely on ride-share services free of discrimination,” said Jesus A. Osete, acting assistant attorney general, in a statement. “We intend to uphold the ADA’s promise that people with disabilities are entitled to equal access in every part of public life, including essential transportation services.”

Lyft firmly rejected the accusations in a statement.

The lawsuit is the latest from the federal government that targets ride-hailing companies for the treatment of would-be riders with disabilities. The administration filed a similar lawsuit against Uber last year, which is ongoing. Uber settled a separate suit in 2022, and Lyft settled a different one in 2020. The companies stress that their policies and in-app tools require that drivers provide ADA accommodations and remind them of the consequences of refusing to do so.

The new lawsuit against Lyft named several examples of people across the country who hailed a ride on the platform but had one—or, in some cases, several—drivers refuse to take them to their destination, including as recently as last month. Those individuals experienced delays in getting to medical appointments, cancellation fees, and other issues as a result, the suit said.

Lyft policies require drivers to accommodate riders who travel with service animals or mobility devices, and “drivers who violate these policies face serious consequences, including permanent deactivation,” the company said in a statement.

“We’ve cooperated with the DOJ throughout its review and remain committed to serving every rider, including riders with disabilities,” the company said.

The lawsuit was filed in U.S. District Court for the Northern District of California. The Department of Justice said it is seeking $53 million for individuals who have been discriminated against and have submitted complaints to Lyft or the department.

—By Hannah Fingerhut, Associated Press

items.title: [euronews.com] Canary Islands receive record 1,488 migrants as Spain declares emergency
items.content_html:
🪶 ✏️

Spanish maritime rescuers assisted 1,488 migrants aboard 14 boats on Saturday, surpassing the previous one-day record of 1,461 set in 2020. Spanish authorities counted 2,331 arrivals across Friday and Saturday. Most of Saturday’s arrivals reached El Hierro, one of the archipelago’s smallest islands. Spain declared a migration emergency in the islands on Nov. 11 after arrivals increased in recent weeks. The Interior Ministry recorded 6,194 arrivals in October, the route’s highest monthly total since 2023. More than 13,000 people reached the Canaries by sea between January and October, 5.5% fewer than in the same period last year. El Hierro’s island council had already declared a social emergency after more than 8,000 arrivals over five weeks, and Canary Islands President Fernando Clavijo appealed to European Commissioner for Migration Magnus Brunner for urgent action. Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez pledged to convene an interministerial immigration commission, while Territorial Policy Minister Ángel Víctor Torres visited the island on Sunday.
